profile.headline: The prototype flavivirus and the reason the genus is named 'flavi' — a vaccine-preventable viral haemorrhagic fever.
profile.syndrome: Biphasic: an initial fever with headache and myalgia, brief remission, then in ~15% a toxic phase with jaundice, haemorrhage, renal failure and shock; case fatality in the toxic phase is 30–60%.
profile.transmission: Urban cycle via Aedes aegypti; sylvatic cycle via Haemagogus and Sabethes mosquitoes with non-human primates.
profile.geography: Tropical South America and sub-Saharan Africa.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR early; IgM serology later; histopathology of liver (Councilman bodies) post-mortem.
profile.prevention: A single dose of the 17D live-attenuated vaccine gives lifelong protection — one of the most effective vaccines ever made; mandated under International Health Regulations for travel to endemic areas.
evidence: Walter Reed Commission human-transmission experiments (1900) and a century of vaccine and surveillance data.

geo.text: Tropical South America and sub-Saharan Africa.

profile.headline: The leading cause of vaccine-preventable viral encephalitis in Asia.
profile.syndrome: Fewer than 1% of infections become clinical, but encephalitis carries ~20–30% mortality and leaves neurological or psychiatric sequelae in a third to a half of survivors; parkinsonian and acute flaccid paralysis presentations are characteristic.
profile.transmission: Culex tritaeniorhynchus in rice-paddy ecosystems; pigs amplify and ardeid water birds maintain the cycle.
profile.reservoir: Ardeid wading birds; pigs as amplifying hosts.
profile.geography: South, Southeast and East Asia, Papua New Guinea, northern Australia.
profile.prevention: Highly effective inactivated and live-attenuated vaccines (e.g. IXIARO, SA 14-14-2) in routine childhood programmes; pig husbandry siting; vector control.
evidence: Large vaccine trials and decades of CSF-confirmed surveillance give unambiguous causal evidence.

geo.text: South, Southeast and East Asia, Papua New Guinea, northern Australia.

profile.headline: Australian member of the Japanese encephalitis serocomplex.
profile.syndrome: Mostly asymptomatic or mild febrile illness; rare encephalitis with high mortality and frequent sequelae, affecting mainly children and older adults.
profile.transmission: Culex annulirostris in wetland and inland floodplain cycles.
profile.geography: Northern and inland Australia, Papua New Guinea; outbreaks follow heavy La Niña rainfall.
profile.diagnosis: CSF/serum IgM; cross-reacts with other JE-serocomplex flaviviruses.
profile.prevention: Mosquito avoidance; sentinel chicken surveillance guides public warnings.
evidence: Confirmed encephalitis cases in Australian epidemics of 1951, 1974 and 2011.

profile.headline: Globally the most widespread encephalitic flavivirus, maintained in a bird–mosquito cycle.
profile.syndrome: About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; 20% develop West Nile fever; <1% develop neuroinvasive disease — meningitis, encephalitis or a poliomyelitis-like acute flaccid paralysis, with substantial mortality and long-term sequelae in older adults.
profile.transmission: Culex mosquitoes; also transfusion, transplantation, and rare vertical and laboratory transmission.
profile.reservoir: Birds (passerines, corvids); humans and horses are dead-end hosts.
profile.geography: Africa, Europe, Middle East, Asia, Australia (Kunjin), and across the Americas since 1999.
profile.diagnosis: CSF and serum IgM; RT-PCR has low sensitivity in immunocompetent patients but is useful in immunosuppressed and in blood-donor screening.
profile.management: Supportive; no proven antiviral or immunotherapy.
profile.prevention: Mosquito control and personal protection; blood-supply nucleic-acid screening; equine vaccines exist but no human vaccine.
evidence: Decades of surveillance with CSF-confirmed neuroinvasive disease and well-documented transfusion transmission.

geo.text: Africa, Europe, Middle East, Asia, Australia (Kunjin), and across the Americas since 1999.

profile.headline: The most important arboviral infection of humans worldwide, with an estimated 100–400 million infections annually.
profile.syndrome: Dengue fever: high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia ('breakbone fever'), rash. A minority progress at defervescence to dengue with warning signs or severe dengue — plasma leakage, shock, haemorrhage and organ impairment. Secondary infection with a different serotype raises severe-disease risk through antibody-dependent enhancement.
profile.transmission: Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus; human–mosquito–human urban cycle with no need for an animal reservoir.
profile.reservoir: Humans (urban cycle); sylvatic primate cycles exist in Asia and West Africa.
profile.geography: Tropics and subtropics worldwide; expanding with vector range.
profile.diagnosis: NS1 antigen and RT-PCR in the first ~5 days; IgM/IgG thereafter. Serial haematocrit and platelet monitoring guide clinical management.
profile.management: No specific antiviral. Careful fluid management per WHO severity categories is the intervention that saves lives; avoid NSAIDs and intramuscular injections.
profile.prevention: Vector control, Wolbachia-based mosquito replacement, and the live-attenuated vaccines CYD-TDV (serostatus-restricted) and TAK-003.
evidence: Over a century of virological, serological and epidemiological confirmation; among the best-characterised human viral infections.

geo.text: Tropics and subtropics worldwide; expanding with vector range.

profile.headline: Tick-borne flavivirus causing haemorrhagic fever in the Western Ghats of India, with the Alkhumra variant on the Arabian peninsula.
profile.syndrome: Abrupt fever with haemorrhage, and in a substantial minority a second phase of meningoencephalitis; case fatality 3–10%.
profile.transmission: Haemaphysalis spinigera tick bite; also handling infected animal carcasses, and for Alkhumra virus contact with infected livestock or raw milk.
profile.reservoir: Small mammals and monkeys (langurs, bonnet macaques — monkey die-offs herald outbreaks).
profile.geography: Karnataka and neighbouring Indian states; Saudi Arabia and Yemen (Alkhumra).
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR and IgM serology at reference laboratories.
profile.prevention: A formalin-inactivated vaccine is used in Karnataka; tick avoidance and acaricide use in forest workers.
evidence: Continuous outbreak documentation since 1957 with virological confirmation.

profile.headline: Principal cause of tick-borne encephalitis in Europe; vaccine-preventable.
profile.syndrome: Often biphasic — a febrile viraemic phase, a symptom-free interval, then meningitis, meningoencephalitis or meningoencephalomyelitis. Mortality ~1–2% for the European subtype with frequent long-term sequelae; the Far Eastern subtype is more severe.
profile.transmission: Ixodes ricinus tick bite; also unpasteurised milk and cheese from infected goats, sheep or cows.
profile.reservoir: Small rodents; ticks maintain the virus transstadially and transovarially.
profile.geography: Central, eastern and northern Europe, expanding northwards and to higher altitudes.
profile.diagnosis: Serum and CSF IgM/IgG; RT-PCR useful only in the early viraemic phase.
profile.management: Supportive; corticosteroids are not of proven benefit.
profile.prevention: Inactivated vaccines (FSME-IMMUN, Encepur) are highly effective; tick checks, pasteurisation of milk.
evidence: Austrian mass-vaccination programme reduced incidence by roughly 90%, a decisive natural experiment.

geo.text: Central, eastern and northern Europe, expanding northwards and to higher altitudes.

profile.headline: Flavivirus whose 2015–2016 American epidemic established it as a human teratogen.
profile.syndrome: Usually mild or asymptomatic: low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia. Congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly, cerebral calcification, ocular and joint anomalies — follows infection in pregnancy. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an established post-infectious complication.
profile.transmission: Aedes mosquitoes; also sexual, vertical and transfusion transmission.
profile.reservoir: Humans in epidemic settings; non-human primates in sylvatic cycles.
profile.diagnosis: RT-PCR on serum and urine (urine positive longer); serology confounded by dengue cross-reactivity, needing plaque-reduction neutralisation.
profile.management: Supportive; pregnancy surveillance with serial fetal ultrasound.
profile.prevention: Vector control, barrier contraception or abstinence after exposure, travel advice in pregnancy. No licensed vaccine.
evidence: Causal link to congenital anomalies established by viral detection in fetal brain tissue, cohort studies and animal models.
